newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bank officials held hostage for third day.
newsitem.headline: French bank officials held hostage for third day.

text.p: Angry workers occupying the Paris headquarters of the doomed Credit Foncier bank held top bank officials hostage for a third day on Sunday after talks failed to halt government plans to shut it down.
The employees, who have been holding bank governor Jerome Meysonnier and other top executives since Friday said both sides had agreed to new talks but no date or time was set.

"We are disappointed. We had been waiting for a sign that the government was willing to change its mind about dismantling the bank, which it did not give," union leader Michel Lamy told Reuters after the talks broke down.
Arthuis told reporters the government would respect the employees' interests and remained open to other options should another buyer for the troubled bank turn up.
But it also had obligations to French taxpayers, he said.
So for the time being, the plan to spin off the bank's housing loans business to property credit group Credit Immobilier and then wind down the rest was the only proposal on the table, he said.
The minister had abandoned weekend travel plans to meet the protestors for talks that went on for several hours on Saturday.

He had initially insisted talks could be held only if they brought the captive governor along with them. But he backed down after bank staff squatting in the ornate building refused to let Meysonnier go unless the government first axed plans to break up the firm, which it rescued from collapse last year.
The workers fear up to 900 job losses at the 145-year-old property lender, which has 3,300 employees.
Arthuis had earlier criticised the worker protest as counterproductive but Meysonnier seemed unperturbed by the occupation of his headquarters by about 100 employees.
"I find this to be a form of brutality which prevents us from going forward, which prevents us from building," Arthuis told France Inter radio on Saturday morning.
But Meysonnier, walking freely about the building and looking relaxed and in fresh clothes despite his night in the bank, reassured reporters that the protest was peaceful.
"The night went well. Everyone was on their best behaviour," Meysonnier said. Police were not called.
Employees said Arthuis' remarks had only aggravated the situation and accused state-appointed Meysonnier and the government of trying to fix the bank's future without them.
"The bosses want to do the negotiating while treating us like less than nothing," complained a man who said he had done 35 years at the venerable bank and could not afford to be named.

The government, which has always appointed the private bank's management because of its role in issuing subsidised loans, intervened directly last year to bail out Credit Foncier following a 1995 loss of 10.8 billion francs ($2.0 billion).

Arthuis launched a preliminary takeover by a state bank and now wants to carry out the second stage of his plan -- spinning off the core business to Credit Immobilier and passing the rest to a state shell company set up to manage its bond loans.
A collapse could have been disastrous for French financial markets, where Credit Foncier was once the second largest issuer of bonds after the state.
